articles.title: Recognising phone scams and what to do
articles.summary: Phone scams cost Australians millions each year. Learn the warning signs and practical steps to protect yourself from fraudulent calls.

sections.heading: How phone scams work
paragraphs: Scammers call pretending to be from trusted organisations like the ATO, your bank, or even the police. They create urgency to pressure you into giving personal information or transferring money.
They may spoof caller IDs to make it look like a legitimate number. Some use robocalls to reach thousands of people at once.

sections.heading: Warning signs to watch for
paragraphs: Look out for these red flags during any phone call:
bullets: Unexpected calls claiming to be from government agencies or banks
Requests for passwords, PINs, or remote access to your computer
Threats of arrest, legal action, or account suspension
Pressure to act immediately or keep the call secret
Requests to transfer money to a 'safe account'

sections.heading: What to do if you receive a suspicious call
paragraphs: Take these practical steps to protect yourself:
bullets: Hang up — no real organisation will mind you being cautious
Find the official number from the organisation's website or a recent bill
Call them back on the official number to verify the request
Never give personal details to someone who called you
Report the scam to Scamwatch at scamwatch.gov.au

articles.title: Protecting yourself from phishing emails and texts
articles.summary: Phishing is the most common way scammers steal personal information. Learn how to spot fake emails and SMS messages before they cause harm.

sections.heading: What is phishing
paragraphs: Phishing is when scammers send emails or text messages pretending to be from a trusted organisation. The goal is to trick you into clicking a link and entering personal information like passwords or bank details.
These messages often look convincing and may include real logos and formatting from the organisation they are impersonating.

sections.heading: How to spot phishing attempts
paragraphs: Common signs of a phishing message include:
bullets: Generic greetings like 'Dear customer' instead of your name
Urgent language like 'Your account will be suspended'
Links that go to unfamiliar or misspelled website addresses
Requests for passwords, credit card numbers, or personal details
Poor grammar and spelling mistakes

sections.heading: Practical steps to stay safe
paragraphs: Follow these actions to protect yourself from phishing:
bullets: Never click links in unexpected emails or texts — go to the website directly
Check the sender's actual email address, not just the display name
Use multi-factor authentication on important accounts
Report phishing emails to ReportCyber at cyber.gov.au
If you've clicked a link, change your password immediately

articles.title: Investment scam red flags everyone should know
articles.summary: Investment scams are the highest-loss scam type in Australia. Learn the warning signs of fake investment opportunities and how to verify them.

sections.heading: Why investment scams succeed
paragraphs: Investment scams promise high returns with little or no risk. They often use professional-looking websites, fake testimonials, and social media advertising to appear legitimate.
Australians lost over $1.3 billion to investment scams in recent years, making it the most costly scam category according to Scamwatch.

sections.heading: Red flags to watch for
paragraphs: Be suspicious of any investment opportunity that shows these signs:
bullets: Guaranteed returns or claims of no risk
Pressure to invest quickly or miss out
Unsolicited contact through social media or messaging apps
Requests to pay using cryptocurrency or gift cards
An unregistered company or financial adviser

sections.heading: How to verify and protect yourself
paragraphs: Before investing any money:
bullets: Check the ASIC register at moneysmart.gov.au to verify the company
Search for the company name plus 'scam' or 'review' online
Never invest based on advice from someone you only know online
Be wary of celebrity endorsements — they are almost always fake
Talk to a licensed independent financial adviser before investing

articles.title: Safe online shopping: avoid fake stores and checkout scams
articles.summary: Fake online stores and checkout scams are increasingly common. Learn how to shop safely online and protect your payment details.

sections.heading: How fake online stores operate
paragraphs: Scammers create professional-looking websites that mimic real retailers. They advertise heavily on social media with prices that look too good to be true. After you pay, the goods either never arrive or are counterfeit.
Some fake stores also harvest your credit card details for later fraudulent use.

sections.heading: Signs of a fake online store
paragraphs: Watch for these warning signs before purchasing:
bullets: Prices significantly below what other retailers charge
No physical address, ABN, or contact phone number listed
Recently created website with no reviews or social media history
Payment only accepted via bank transfer, crypto, or gift cards
Poor website design, broken links, or copied product descriptions

sections.heading: How to shop safely online
paragraphs: Follow these practices for safer online shopping:
bullets: Use trusted well-known retailers when possible
Pay with credit card or PayPal for buyer protection
Search the store name on scamwatch.gov.au before purchasing
Look for the ABN and verify it at abr.business.gov.au
If a deal seems too good to be true, it probably is

articles.title: Protecting older Australians from scams
articles.summary: Older Australians are frequently targeted by scammers. This guide covers common tactics used against seniors and practical steps families can take.

sections.heading: Why older Australians are targeted
paragraphs: Scammers target older Australians because they may be less familiar with digital technology, more trusting of authority figures, and often have retirement savings. Common scams targeting seniors include remote access scams, romance scams, and impersonation of government agencies.
The eSafety Commissioner reports that older Australians lose more money per scam incident than younger age groups.

sections.heading: Common scams targeting seniors
paragraphs: Be aware of these frequently used tactics:
bullets: Remote access scams where callers ask to control your computer
Romance scams through dating sites or social media
Grandparent scams where someone pretends to be a family member in trouble
Fake tech support claiming your computer has a virus
Medicare or Centrelink impersonation demanding personal details

sections.heading: What families can do to help
paragraphs: Practical steps to protect older family members:
bullets: Have regular open conversations about common scams without judgement
Help set up call blocking and spam filters on their phone
Establish a family code word to verify emergency requests
Encourage them to check with family before making large payments
Report any suspected scams to Scamwatch together

articles.title: Securing your devices and online accounts
articles.summary: Strong security on your devices and accounts is your first line of defence against scammers. Learn the practical basics that make the biggest difference.

sections.heading: Why device and account security matters
paragraphs: Many scams succeed because attackers gain access to poorly secured accounts or devices. A compromised email account can be used to reset other passwords, access banking, and impersonate you to friends and family.
The Australian Cyber Security Centre recommends a few core practices that stop the majority of common attacks.

sections.heading: Essential security checklist
paragraphs: Focus on these high-impact actions first:
bullets: Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA) for email, banking, and social media
Use a unique strong password for every important account
Keep your phone and computer software updated — enable automatic updates
Lock your phone with a PIN, fingerprint, or face recognition
Only install apps from official app stores

sections.heading: What to do if you think you have been compromised
paragraphs: If you suspect your account or device has been accessed by someone else:
bullets: Change your passwords immediately, starting with email
Check your account activity and sign out of unrecognised sessions
Contact your bank if financial accounts may be affected
Report the incident to ReportCyber at cyber.gov.au
Run a security scan on your device with reputable antivirus software
